hops.title: Your cortical neurons skip the seven-year replacement
hops.text: People love to say every cell in your body is replaced every seven years. Cold War bomb tests showed that the neurons of your neocortex break that rule. Above-ground nuclear tests sent atmospheric carbon-14 soaring worldwide, and levels fell sharply after 1963. Cells copying their DNA took up carbon-14 from food, so the new strands tracked atmospheric levels with a short lag. In 2005 and 2006, Kirsty Spalding, Ratan Bhardwaj, Jonas Frisén and colleagues measured it in adult human brains. Non-neuronal cells had turned over. Neocortical neurons carried the carbon-14 of the time around the person's birth: made in development, and not replaced in adulthood at detectable levels.

sources.citation: Spalding KL, Bhardwaj RD, Buchholz BA, Druid H, Frisén J. Retrospective birth dating of cells in humans. Cell 122(1):133-143 (2005).
Bhardwaj RD et al. Neocortical neurogenesis in humans is restricted to development. Proc Natl Acad Sci U S A 103(33):12564-12568 (2006).

hops.afterHeading: Cause or record? Moving a birthday
hops.title: Human neurons in a mouse brain keep human time
hops.text: Mouse cortical neurons mature in weeks; human ones take months to years. So what happens when human neurons grow up inside a mouse? In 2013 and 2019, Pierre Vanderhaeghen's team grafted developing human cortical cells derived from embryonic stem cells into newborn mouse brains. In the 2019 study the human cells wired into mouse visual cortex, and some responded selectively when the mouse watched moving stripes. Yet they matured over months, on a human schedule, while the host grew up around them. In 2023 the group traced part of that slow clock to the neurons' own mitochondria: boosting mitochondrial metabolism made human neurons mature weeks ahead of schedule.

sources.citation: Espuny-Camacho I et al. Pyramidal neurons derived from human pluripotent stem cells integrate efficiently into mouse brain circuits in vivo. Neuron 77(3):440-456 (2013).
Linaro D et al. Xenotransplanted human cortical neurons reveal species-specific development and functional integration into mouse visual circuits. Neuron 104(5):972-986 (2019).
Iwata R et al. Mitochondria metabolism sets the species-specific tempo of neuronal development. Science 379(6632):eabn4705 (2023).

image.caption: Grafted human cortical cells wired into mouse cortex, some responding to moving stripes, yet matured on a human clock.

hops.title: A marsupial clue to how axons choose a route between hemispheres
hops.text: Your two hemispheres talk across the corpus callosum, a thick axon bridge. Marsupials have none. Their hemispheres connect through a lower route, the anterior commissure. In 2020, Annalisa Paolino, Linda Richards, Rodrigo Suárez and colleagues compared mice with an Australian marsupial, the fat-tailed dunnart. Both use the same identity genes, Satb2 and Ctip2. One difference was timing: SATB2 protein becomes detectable at an earlier developmental stage in dunnarts than in mice. Expressing extra Satb2 early in mouse embryos sent more cortical axons through the anterior commissure, the marsupial route. Added later, it reduced projections to the matching area of the opposite cortex with no detectable increase in anterior-commissure axons.

sources.citation: Paolino A, Fenlon LR, Kozulin P, Haines E, Lim JWC, Richards LJ, Suárez R. Differential timing of a conserved transcriptional network underlies divergent cortical projection routes across mammalian brain evolution. Proc Natl Acad Sci U S A 117(19):10554-10564 (2020).

image.caption: Early extra Satb2 sent more mouse cortical axons through the anterior commissure, the route marsupials use.

audio.title: Three true stories about neuron birthdays
audio.transcript:
Here are three true stories about timing in the cortex: when neurons are born, how fast they mature, and when a key identity protein appears.

First, you have probably heard that every cell in your body is replaced every seven years. The neurons of your neocortex are a clear exception, and the evidence came, of all places, from Cold War nuclear weapons testing. Above-ground bomb tests sent atmospheric carbon fourteen soaring across the whole planet, and then levels fell steeply after nineteen sixty-three. Cells copying their D N A built in carbon fourteen from food, so the new strands tracked atmospheric carbon fourteen with a short lag. In two thousand five and two thousand six, Kirsty Spalding, Ratan Bhardwaj, Jonas Frisén and their colleagues at the Karolinska Institute measured that carbon fourteen in adult human brains. The non-neuronal cells had turned over. The neurons of the neocortex still carried the carbon fourteen of the time around the person's birth. It is the same logic as a pulse of radioactive thymidine in a mouse embryo, except the pulse was the whole atmosphere. Comparing the carbon fourteen in their D N A with the atmospheric record dated those neurons to around the person's birth, and found no detectable replacement in adulthood.

Second, what happens if you put developing human cortical cells into a newborn mouse brain? Mouse cortical neurons mature in a matter of weeks. Human ones take months to years. You might expect the fast mouse surroundings to hurry the human cells along. In two thousand thirteen, Pierre Vanderhaeghen's laboratory reported grafting a mix of human cortical progenitors and neurons, derived from embryonic stem cells, into newborn mice. In a second study, in two thousand nineteen, the human neurons wired into the mouse visual cortex and received input from the host, and some responded selectively to stripes moving in particular directions. They still refused to hurry. They matured over many months, on a human schedule, while the mouse brain grew up around them. In two thousand twenty-three, the same group found part of that slow timer inside the cells' own mitochondria, which run at a lower metabolic rate in human neurons. Boosting mitochondrial metabolism made the human neurons mature weeks ahead of schedule.

Third, timing does more than set how fast a neuron grows up. It can change the route an axon takes between the two halves of the brain. In mice and humans, many neurons that switch on a gene called Sat b two, especially in the upper layers, send their axons across the corpus callosum, the large bridge of axons that links the left and right hemispheres. Marsupials, such as the opossum, build a six-layered cortex too, yet marsupials have no corpus callosum at all. Their hemispheres connect through a lower route called the anterior commissure. In two thousand twenty, Annalisa Paolino, Linda Richards, Rodrigo Suárez and their colleagues compared mice with an Australian marsupial, the fat-tailed dunnart. Both animals use the same identity genes, Sat b two and C tip two. One difference was timing: the Sat b two protein becomes detectable in the developing cortex at an earlier stage in dunnarts than in mice. When the researchers made mouse embryos express extra Sat b two early, to mimic the dunnart's schedule, more cortical axons took the anterior commissure, the marsupial route. At the later stage tested, extra Sat b two reduced projections to the matching area of the opposite cortex, with no detectable increase in axons entering the anterior commissure. Same factor, earlier timing, a shift in wiring.
